analysis.one_liner: Creates a national health insurance program covering all residents, with set budgets, fee schedules, and Canadian-style drug price limits.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to six House committees in September 1992 and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote; it had no cosponsors and died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required every legal resident to enroll in a federally approved health insurance policy covering hospital care, doctor visits, dental, mental health, and vision services. A new Federal Health Board would set one national premium per family category, subsidize premiums fully or partially for low-income people, set fee schedules for doctors through state-chartered practitioner associations, and give each hospital district an annual global budget. It would cap drug prices at Canadian levels, repeal Medicare, Medicaid, CHAMPUS, and the federal employees' health program once the new system was running, and pay for part of it with sharply higher taxes on cigarettes and liquor. It never got past the committee referral stage.
analysis.who_benefits: All legal residents would gain guaranteed coverage, with free or reduced premiums for people at or near the federal poverty line and free coverage for enrolled Native Americans. Patients would keep freedom to choose practitioners and could buy extra private insurance for uncovered services.

how_it_helps.text: Requires every legal resident of the United States to be enrolled in an approved health insurance policy, with states randomly assigning anyone who fails to enroll, establishing universal coverage.

Guarantees coverage of all necessary and appropriate practitioner services — medical, chiropractic, dental, mental health, and vision — anywhere in the United States, ending coverage gaps that leave people unable to get care.

Provides a 100 percent premium reduction for individuals and families at or below the federal poverty line, a sliding-scale reduction up to ten income units above the poverty line, and free premiums for enrolled members of federally recognized tribes.
Caps pharmaceutical and health device prices at the levels permitted in Canada by the Patented Medicine Review Board, effective January 1, 1993.
Requires doctors to accept the negotiated fee schedule as payment in full (mandatory assignment), ending balance billing of patients above the agreed rate.
Sets annual global budgets for each health care district and national per capita spending rates, an explicit mechanism to hold total health spending down.

analysis.who_pays: Private insurers would lose control of premium pricing and policy terms, all subject to Federal Health Board approval. Drug makers would be limited to Canadian prices. Tobacco and liquor companies and their customers would face excise tax increases (cigarettes roughly rising from $12 to $30.50 per thousand, liquor from $13.50 to $50 per proof gallon). Hospitals would operate under fixed annual budgets. Doctors would have to accept fee-schedule rates as payment in full, and malpractice punitive damages would be eliminated.
analysis.who_pays_short: Insurers, drug makers, hospitals, smokers and drinkers

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals Medicare, Medicaid, CHAMPUS, and the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program once the new system takes effect (October 1, 1998), so the entire existing public coverage system is replaced by an untested one — a major transition risk for seniors and federal workers.
The antitrust laws would not apply to hospitals and other health entities contracting with state boards, removing competition oversight precisely when the bill consolidates purchasing power.

The bill prohibits punitive damages in all medical malpractice claims and shifts liability from individual practitioners to their associations, weakening the main legal remedy for patients injured by negligent care.

Fixed global district budgets and mandatory fee schedules could mean waiting lists or reduced access to services if funding lagged demand, since districts could not pay more than their approved budget outside emergencies.

Federal Health Board control of one national premium per enrollment category, plus state fee-setting, would concentrate enormous pricing power in appointed boards with little direct electoral accountability.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would guarantee universal coverage and strong drug price and spending controls — a large gain for ordinary people — but it does so by replacing Medicare, Medicaid, and other proven programs with an entirely new federal-state structure, and it buys provider cooperation with an antitrust exemption and the abolition of malpractice punitive damages, real costs to patients and competition that an honest supporter would have to acknowledge.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with no cosponsors on September 24, 1992, referred to six House committees and scattered among six subcommittees, and none of them ever acted on it before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

narrative.text: Rep. Collin Peterson of Minnesota introduced the Comprehensive Health Care and Cost Containment Act of 1992 on September 24, 1992.

The bill was referred jointly to six House committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Judiciary, Education and Labor, Armed Services, and Post Office and Civil Service — reflecting how many parts of health policy it touched.

Within three weeks it was further divided among six subcommittees, including the Subcommittee on Health and the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment; no committee or subcommittee ever reported it, held a hearing, or brought it to a vote.
The 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993, and the bill died without ever reaching the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers, the pharmaceutical industry, and the existing employer-based insurance system all came out ahead, since nothing about premium pricing, drug prices, or coverage changed. The 33-plus million uninsured Americans the bill identified gained nothing; the problem it described continued into the next decade of health reform fights.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and drug makers; the uninsured gained nothing

for.name: Rep. Collin C. Peterson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on September 24, 1992, its sole sponsor.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Judiciary, Education and Labor, Armed Services, and Post Office and Civil Service Committees
against.role: The six committees to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearings, no markups, no report to the floor — before the Congress ended.

against.name: The health insurance, pharmaceutical, and hospital industries
against.role: Industries whose pricing power and market roles the bill would have curtailed
against.what_they_did: Opposed comprehensive national health insurance proposals during the early-1990s health reform debate, which culminated instead in the defeat of the Clinton health plan in 1994.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a floor vote and drew no cosponsors, so no party or faction ever went on record for or against it.

industries.note: The bill keeps private insurers as the issuers of approved policies under a universal enrollment mandate, but strips them of pricing power: the Federal Health Board must approve every premium and policy, and standardized claim forms replace their administrative practices. They would survive as permanent gatekeepers of the national program while losing the freedom to price and design coverage.

Manufacturers could not charge U.S. prices above what Canada's Patented Medicine Review Board permits, directly cutting revenue in their highest-priced market. Consumers would pay less for prescription drugs.

industries.industry: Hospitals, nursing homes, and other care facilities
industries.note: Facilities would gain guaranteed payment through district contracts and global budgets, plus an antitrust exemption for contracting with government boards — but their total revenue would be capped by fixed annual budgets they could not exceed outside emergencies.

Doctors would negotiate fee schedules through state-chartered associations and escape individual malpractice liability and punitive damages, but would have to accept the fee schedule as payment in full — giving up balance billing of patients.

industries.industry: Tobacco and distilled spirits producers and retailers
industries.note: Cigarette taxes would roughly rise from $12 to $30.50 per thousand and liquor taxes from $13.50 to $50.00 per proof gallon, with floor-stock taxes on inventory held on January 1, 1995. The revenue funds the Health Care Education Trust Fund, and higher prices would discourage smoking and drinking — a cost the industries pass to their customers.
